column3: Parent+offspring pool sorted by non-dominated rank, ties broken by crowding distance, binary tournament mating (elitist).
column4: • Elitist and nearly parameter-free: P3 HV 0.487, IGD 0.032 †.; • Very even spread through crowding distance: Spacing 0.014 (P3) and 0.005 (P6) †.; • Fast: 0.4s for 10,000 evaluations †.; • Handles real, permutation and binary variables with suitable operators (P8, P9).; • Excellent two- and three-objective baseline.
column5: • Collapses on 5 objectives: P10 (M=5) HV 0.131, IGD 0.655 vs NSGA-III's HV 0.488 †.; • At M=5 a random population is already 57% non-dominated (study), so ranking cannot select †.; • Crowding distance is meaningless when most points are non-dominated in many dimensions.; • O(M N²) sorting per generation.; • Constraints only through penalty unless the constrained variant is used.
column6: 2–3 objective problems with up to a few thousand evaluations (P3, P5, P6).

column3: NSGA-II-style survival with crowding replaced by reference points: normalise, associate to reference lines, fill the least crowded niches.
column4: • Keeps spread in many objectives: P10 (M=5) HV 0.488 vs NSGA-II 0.131 †.; • On 3 objectives gets 92 points, IGD 0.104 †.; • Reference points give a predefined well-spread target distribution.; • Adaptive normalisation copes with differently scaled objectives.; • Same operators as NSGA-II.
column5: • Slow convergence at M = 5 in 10,000 evaluations: IGD 0.496, mean solution still outside the unit sphere †.; • Number of reference points (and hence N) grows combinatorially with M and divisions p.; • Assumes a simplex-like front; irregular fronts leave empty reference lines.; • Normalisation (extreme points, intercepts) is fragile – fallbacks needed.; • Slower per generation than NSGA-II (0.6s on M=3) †.
column7: Disconnected or strongly degenerate fronts, tiny budgets.

column3: Fitness = raw (sum of strengths of dominators) + density from the k-th nearest neighbour; fixed-size archive truncated by nearest-neighbour distance.
column4: • Even, dense fronts: P4 Spacing 0.003, IGD 0.004 †.; • Fitness distinguishes dominated individuals as well (fine-grained).; • Archive guarantees elitism and constant size.; • Density from k-th neighbour scales with the population.; • Works unchanged with penalty constraints (P5: 100 points, HV 0.815) †.
column5: • Heavy: 2.3s for 10,000 evaluations vs 0.4s for NSGA-II †.; • O(n³) archive truncation in the worst case.; • P5 IGD 0.013 is worse than NSGA-II's 0.013 †.; • Fitness needs full strength/raw computation each generation (O(n²M)).; • Density estimator also degrades with many objectives.
column6: 2–3 objective problems where the archive quality matters (P4).
column7: Tight time budgets or many objectives.

column3: External archive on an adaptive grid; selection picks a hyper-box (less crowded preferred) then a member in it.
column4: • Region-based selection is cheap to maintain (grid index) and gives 100 points on P3 †.; • Good IGD 0.009 on P3 †.; • Archive is bounded; crowded boxes are thinned automatically.; • Few evaluations per generation allow fast adaptation.; • Insensitive to objective scales (grid is rescaled).
column5: • Grid resolution is a sensitive parameter (10 divisions here); too fine → many empty boxes, too coarse → no pressure.; • Slower than NSGA-II in Python (3.2s vs 0.4s) because of per-generation grid/archive updates †.; • P5 IGD 0.021 vs NSGA-II 0.013 †.; • Grid size grows as div^M – unusable for many objectives.; • Small internal population (20) limits exploration.

column3: N weight vectors define N Tchebycheff sub-problems; each is improved with children bred from neighbouring sub-problems, and solved children replace neighbours.
column4: • Accurate and even: P3 IGD 0.610, Spacing nan †.; • Handles three objectives (P10: HV 0.679) †.; • O(MNT) per generation – no sorting.; • Tchebycheff reaches non-convex fronts.; • Weights give direct control of where points lie.
column5: • Returned only 1 of 100 sub-problem solutions on P3 (several sub-problems share a solution) †.; • Needs weights/neighbourhood T/nr/δ; slow in Python (3.5s) †.; • Uniform weights do not give uniform points on irregular fronts.; • Needs ideal/nadir estimates (here the current population) that can mislead early on.; • Weaker than NSGA-III on 3-objective P10 (IGD 0.087 vs 0.104 with fewer points) †.
column6: Smooth fronts with many objectives; when preferences map to weights.

column3: MOEA/D whose variation is differential evolution (x_r1 + F(x_r2 − x_r3)) with polynomial mutation and a limit nr on replacements.
column4: • Best IGD on P3 among the decomposition runs: 0.005, Spacing 0.003 †.; • Dense front on P3: 96 points †.; • DE steps adapt to the scale of the neighbourhood.; • nr limit protects diversity.; • No crossover distribution index to tune.
column5: • On P5 worse than NSGA-II: IGD 0.034 vs 0.013, Spacing 0.037 †.; • Real-valued only (not for permutations/bits).; • Python cost 4.5s for 10,000 evaluations †.; • F and CR matter; CR=1 destroys separability.; • Same weight/neighbourhood parameters as MOEA/D.
column6: Continuous problems with complicated Pareto sets (P3).

column3: MOEA/D where each sub-problem has its own pheromone matrix; ants build tours, neighbouring sub-problems share information.
column4: • Finds the whole 10-point front of P8 (HV 0.757) †.; • Decomposition gives each ant a clear scalar target.; • Heuristic information specific to each weight vector.; • Pheromone sharing among neighbours speeds up search.; • Cheap on a 15-city instance (3.9s) †.
column5: • Slower than NSGA-II in wall-clock (3.9s vs 0.7s for NSGA-II on P8) †.; • Parameters: α, β, ρ, T, number of sub-problems.; • One pheromone matrix per sub-problem: O(N n²) memory.; • Permutation problems only.; • No benefit shown over simple operators on only 15 cities (same front as MOACO and NSGA-II) †.
column6: Larger routing problems where good heuristics exist.
